title: Biopsy  proteome score performs well as an effect measure in a gluten-challenge trial of coeliac disease
projectDescription: Objective Development of novel treatments for coeliac disease (CeD) is dependent on precise tools to monitor changes in gluten-induced mucosal damage. Current histology measures are subjective and difficult to standardise. Biopsy proteome scoring is an objective alternative to histology which is based on robust changes in biological pathways that directly reflect gluten-induced mucosal damage. In this study we aimed to evaluate biopsy proteome scoring as effect measure in a clinical trial setting by measuring intestinal remodeling in response to oral gluten challenge.  Design We analyzed biopsies from a gluten challenge trial of treated CeD patients that consumed 3 g (n=6) or 10 g (n=7) gluten per day for 14 days. Sections from individually embedded biopsies collected before and after challenge were processed for proteome scoring (n = 109) and measurement of Vh:Cd ratio (n = 58). Proteome scores were compared to histology, intraepithelial lymphocyte (IEL) frequency and plasma interleukin-2 (IL-2).  Results Change in proteome scores were significant for the group of patients who consumed 10 g gluten, but not for the group who consumed 3 g gluten. Altogether, 8  of 13 patients had changes in delta proteome scores above cut-off. Proteome scores correlated with Vh:Cd ratios both at run-in and at day 15. Proteome scores at day 15 correlated with IEL frequency and with serum IL-2 levels measured 4 hours post gluten intake. Conclusion Biopsy proteome scoring is a simple and reliable measure of gluten-induced mucosal remodeling in response to 14-day oral gluten challenge.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Protein extraction from FFPE tissue sections Glass-mounted FFPE tissue sections were deparaffinised in xylene followed by sequential rehydration in EtOH and water before drying. The tissue was scraped off the glass slides and collected in PCR tubes containing 25 µl 100 mM ammonium bicarbonate with 0.1 % ProteaseMAX Surfactant (Promega, Madison, WI) and 10 mM DTT (HPLC-grade, Sigma) followed by incubation at 96 °C for 90 minutes. The samples were ultrasonicated for 60 minutes (Branson Ultrasonics, Brookfield, CT), alkylated with 10 mM iodoacetamide (Sigma) at 22 °C for 30 minutes in the dark and digested with 0.2 µg trypsin (sequencing grade, ProMega, Madison, WI) at 37 °C overnight. The resulting digests were acidified with 0.5 % formic acid (FA)  and 3 µl sample digest was applied to Evotips (Evosep, Odense, Denmark) for clean-up prior to liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis.  LC-MS measurements Tissue digests were analyzed by ultra-high-performance LC (UHPLC)  and trapped ion mobility spectrometry (tims) time-of-flight (TOF)  MS using the Evosep One system (Evosep, Odense, Denmark) connected to a timsTOFfleX mass spectrometer via a CaptiveSpray ion source (Bruker Daltonics, Bremen, Germany).  The peptides were separated on an Evosep analytical column (Dr Maisch, column length 15 cm, 150 µm inner diameter, 1.9 µm C18 AQ beads) using the manufacturer’s predefined Evosep 30 samples per day (SPD) protocol with a 44 min gradient with 0.1 % FA and 0.1 % FA in acetonitrile. The mass spectrometer was operated in data-dependent parallel accumulation-serial fragmentation (PASEF) mode recording mass spectra for MS and MS/MS scans between 100-1700 m/z. The ion mobility resolution was 0.60-1.60 V s cm−2 over a 100 ms ramp time. For data-dependent acquisition we used ten PASEF MS/MS scans per cycle with a near 100 % duty cycle. To exclude low m/z singly charged ions from the PASEF precursor selection a polygon filter in the m/z and ion mobility space was applied. We used an active exclusion time of 0.4 minutes to precursors that reached 20 000 intensity units. Collisional energy was ramped stepwise as a function of ion mobility.
dataProcessingProtocol: Protein identification and quantification MS instrument raw files were searched against the human UniProt KB database (version of January 2022) using MaxQuant (v2.0.3.0) 9. Protein FDR and  protein spectrum match were set to 1 % and the minimum number of razor + unique peptides used for identification was one. We used trypsin as digestion enzyme with maximum two missed cleavages. Methionine oxidation and N-terminus acetylation were added as variable modifications, carbamidomethylation as a fixed modification with maximum five modifications per peptide. Proteins were quantified by intensity-based absolute quantification (iBAQ) using  a minimum number of razor peptides of one.   Data processing for proteome score calculations The search output files  from MaxQuant were processed with the R Statistical Software (v4.2.0 and 4.2.3) 10 using the RStudio environment 11. Potential contaminants, proteins present in the reverse decoy database search, proteins without annotated gene names, identified by site, with no unique peptide or with missing iBAQ values were removed. In cases with several entries per protein group,  one protein was kept according to the principle of parsimony. Three of the 109  analyzed samples had less than 1000 iBAQ quantified proteins and were excluded, resulting in further analysis on biopsies from 16 patients at run-in and 13 patients post gluten challenge.
